scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Okumkpa is an African dance and theatrical tradition preserved among the Igbo Afikpo communities in Nigeria.
Documented in ethnographic studies by scholars such as Herbert M. Cole, the tradition operates as an established post-harvest and dry-season social commentary.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Okumkpa is typically performed following the Dry Season Festival.

It carries deep satirical and moral meaning, featuring humorous critiques of foolish behavior, including enactments of contests to determine the most foolish man on earth who wins the Pot of Foolishness.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dancers wear individually named carved wooden masks that facilitate their transformation into mma (spirits).
Performances take place in community village settings, with documented historical masks archived in collections such as the Seattle Art Museum.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Scholar Herbert M. Cole documented key aspects of the Okumkpa masquerade and its leadership contexts in African Art and Leadership.
The tradition is rooted specifically among the Afikpo Igbo groups of southeastern Nigeria.
Okumkpa forms part of the broader Igbo masking and masquerade lineage, in which performers become mma to enact community drama and social regulation.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Performers wear masks to transform into mma (ancestral spirits). Outsiders should observe local protocols regarding spirit impersonation and the sacred nature of Igbo masquerades.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: In Afikpo, masked dancers channel spirits to stage a biting, hilarious pageant where human folly is exposed for the entire town.
